title: A $2 Tuberculosis Vaccine Just Normalised Blood Sugar in Type 1 Diabetics. South Asians Should Pay Attention.
excerpt: BCG shots reprogrammed malfunctioning white blood cells and slashed insulin use in adults with lifelong Type 1 diabetes — bypassing the pancreas entirely.
body:
Every Indian child born in a government hospital receives it within hours of birth. The BCG vaccine — a century-old tuberculosis shot that costs roughly two dollars — has just produced one of the most striking diabetes results in decades, and the mechanism has nothing to do with the pancreas.

At the American Diabetes Association meeting in New Orleans this month, Dr Denise Faustman of Massachusetts General Hospital presented data from a mid-stage trial showing that six BCG injections over five years dramatically improved blood sugar control in adults who have lived with Type 1 diabetes since childhood. Continuous glucose monitoring showed up to a 183.7 per cent improvement over baseline in time spent within the normal blood sugar range — without a single extra episode of dangerous hypoglycaemia.

"Many patients in the trial were able to normalise their blood sugar levels," the researchers reported.

A Metabolic Defect, Not Just an Immune One

The conventional understanding of Type 1 diabetes is that the immune system attacks the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. Most research has focused on stopping that autoimmune assault. But Faustman's work reveals a parallel problem that has been hiding in plain sight.

"White blood cells in people with Type 1 diabetes have a metabolic defect," she said. "Their white blood cells consume fat in the blood for fuel." In healthy people, those same cells consume sugar. If white blood cells are not utilising and regulating blood glucose, abnormal blood sugar levels persist — independent of the pancreas.

In the trial, 34 adults received BCG shots while 24 received placebo injections. The BCG immunotherapy activated a cascade of events that reprogrammed the malfunctioning white blood cells, switching their fuel source back from fat to sugar. The placebo group saw no such improvement.

Why This Matters More Than You Think

Unlike insulin injections — which can cause blood sugar to plunge and then rebound dangerously — properly functioning white blood cells keep glucose closer to normal for longer stretches. Faustman called BCG "a safe drug that with limited dosing restores blood sugars to a normal range."

The implications are enormous. More than 100 million newborns receive BCG each year, according to the World Health Organization. The vaccine has over a century of safety data. It is already approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for tuberculosis vaccination and bladder cancer treatment. If larger trials confirm these results, a drug that already exists in virtually every hospital on Earth could transform how Type 1 diabetes is managed.

The South Asian Dimension

India alone has more than 1.1 million people living with Type 1 diabetes, and the country has the second-highest incidence in the world among children under 14. For the diaspora, this matters on two fronts.

First, South Asian children diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes in the US, UK and Canada face a lifetime of insulin dependence, continuous glucose monitors and pump management. A therapy that reprograms immune metabolism rather than replacing a hormone could fundamentally change their prognosis.

Second, BCG is manufactured on a massive scale by the Serum Institute of India in Pune — the same facility that became a household name during the Covid-19 vaccine rollout. If BCG's diabetes application reaches Phase 3 trials and eventually wins approval, India is positioned to be both a major beneficiary and a supplier.

What Comes Next

This was a Phase 2 trial with 58 participants. Larger, multi-centre Phase 3 trials are needed before BCG could be approved for diabetes. Faustman's lab at Massachusetts General is also running a paediatric trial in children with new-onset Type 1 diabetes, testing whether earlier intervention produces even stronger results.

For now, the data is a proof of concept — but a powerful one. A vaccine that most South Asians already carry in their immune memory may hold the key to a disease that disproportionately affects their community. The irony is hard to miss: one of modern medicine's oldest tools may be its newest diabetes treatment.

Sources: Reuters, American Diabetes Association 2026 Scientific Sessions, Massachusetts General Hospital, ClinicalTrials.gov
